name: Calcium
summary: Calcium is the main mineral in bones and teeth, and the body also needs it for muscles, nerves and blood clotting. The body keeps the blood level steady by taking calcium from bone when intake is low. Trials of calcium supplements found small effects on bone density, weak and inconsistent effects on fractures, and some possible harms.
roles: Builds and maintains bones and teeth (about 99% of the body's calcium is there)
Release of hormones and other messengers from cells

status.note: There is no simple test of calcium intake, and this app has no calcium marker. Blood calcium is kept in a narrow range by hormones (parathyroid hormone and vitamin D), which draw calcium from bone when intake is low, so a normal blood calcium does not show that intake is enough. A doctor may check blood calcium (often adjusted for albumin), parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, or bone density with a DXA scan (a low-dose X-ray). These show problems with calcium balance or bone health, not how much calcium someone eats.

signs: Low intake usually causes no symptoms at first, because calcium is taken from bone
Over years: lower bone density and a higher chance of osteoporosis
Low blood calcium (hypocalcaemia), usually from hormone, vitamin D or kidney problems rather than diet: tingling around the mouth or in the fingers, muscle cramps and spasms
atRisk: People who eat no dairy and no calcium-fortified alternatives (for example some vegans, or people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy)
People with low vitamin D, which reduces calcium absorption
Women after menopause, who lose bone faster
Older adults, who absorb calcium less well
People with coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease or after weight-loss surgery
Populations with low calcium diets, which are common in many low- and middle-income countries

signs: Constipation, bloating and wind (common with supplements)
Too much calcium in the blood (hypercalcaemia): nausea, thirst, passing a lot of urine, tiredness, confusion
Milk-alkali syndrome: high calcium, kidney problems and alkaline blood from large amounts of calcium carbonate, often as antacids
high.note: High blood calcium from food alone is rare. It happens mainly with supplements or calcium-containing antacids, especially together with high amounts of vitamin D, or because of a medical condition (overactive parathyroid glands, some cancers). In the Women's Health Initiative trial, calcium with vitamin D raised the risk of kidney stones.

examples: Tofu set with calcium (calcium sulphate or calcium chloride)
Canned fish eaten with the soft bones, such as sardines, pilchards and salmon
Green vegetables such as kale, pak choi, spring greens and broccoli
Bread and other foods made with calcium-fortified flour (white flour in the UK is fortified)
Hard tap water and some mineral waters
foodSources.note: How much calcium the body absorbs differs between foods. Oxalate (in spinach and rhubarb) and phytate (in bran and some seeds) bind calcium, so spinach supplies far less usable calcium than its content suggests.

forms.name: Calcium carbonate
forms.note: The most common and cheapest form, with about 40% calcium by weight. It needs stomach acid, so it is absorbed best with food. It is also the active ingredient of many antacids, which count towards total intake.

forms.name: Calcium citrate
forms.note: About 21% calcium, so tablets are larger or more numerous. It is absorbed with or without food and is often preferred for people with low stomach acid or on acid-reducing medicines.

forms.name: Calcium lactate and gluconate
forms.note: Contain much less calcium per gram, so they are less practical as supplements.

forms.name: Hydroxyapatite, algae, coral or bone-derived calcium
forms.note: Marketed as natural forms. Research on how well they work is limited.

forms.name: Calcium with vitamin D
forms.note: Most fracture trials used combined products. The label's 'elemental calcium' is the amount of calcium itself, not the weight of the whole compound. The body absorbs a larger share of smaller amounts, so a large amount at once is absorbed less efficiently.

intake.group: Adults 25 years and over (men and women)
Pregnancy or breastfeeding, 25 years and over

upperLimit.note: From food and supplements together, for adults including during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Set by the EU's Scientific Committee on Food in 2003 and confirmed by EFSA (the European Food Safety Authority) in 2012, because long trials found total intakes of 2500 mg a day were tolerated without harm. EFSA keeps the same intake value in pregnancy and breastfeeding because the body adapts its handling of calcium during these times.

interactions.note: Calcium and phosphate balance changes in kidney disease and is usually managed by the kidney team; some phosphate binders contain calcium and count towards intake. Talk to your doctor before using calcium supplements.
EFSA's intake value is the same in pregnancy. Calcium to lower the risk of pre-eclampsia is a decision for the midwife or doctor, and the evidence is strongest for low calcium diets.
In a small study, calcium carbonate taken together with levothyroxine lowered thyroid hormone levels and raised TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone). Pharmacists usually advise keeping them hours apart.

interactions.with: Some antibiotics (tetracyclines such as doxycycline, quinolones such as ciprofloxacin)
interactions.note: Calcium binds these antibiotics in the gut and makes them work less well if taken at the same time.
Calcium blocks their absorption when taken together; the leaflet explains the timing.
Calcium taken at the same time can reduce iron absorption.

interactions.with: Thiazide diuretics (water tablets such as bendroflumethiazide)
interactions.note: They reduce calcium lost in urine, so high calcium intake can raise blood calcium.
Vitamin D is needed to absorb calcium. High amounts of both together raise the chance of high blood calcium and kidney stones.
They count towards total calcium intake; large amounts over time can cause milk-alkali syndrome.

cautions: Check the elemental calcium on the label: that is the amount that counts, not the weight of the compound.
Count calcium from food, fortified foods, antacids and supplements together against the upper limit.
Many medicines need to be kept apart from calcium in time; a pharmacist can check yours.
A history of kidney stones, kidney disease or high blood calcium is a reason to talk to a doctor before using calcium supplements.

commonUses: May strengthen bones and prevent fractures
May lower the risk of pre-eclampsia in pregnancy

origin: Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body, about 99 % of it in bones and teeth. It comes from dairy foods, fortified plant drinks, canned fish eaten with the bones, some greens and seeds, and in some places hard tap water.

Supplement calcium is a manufactured salt, such as carbonate or citrate. Calcium alpha-ketoglutarate, a form sold for bone health, is a newer product; this guide has not reviewed human evidence for that form.
dosage: EFSA's reference intake for adults is 950 mg a day from age 25 (1,000 mg at 18 to 24). The upper limit is 2,500 mg a day from food and supplements together. These are population values, not personal targets.
An amount commonly used in supplements is about 1,200 mg a day in total. This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.
Check the elemental calcium in mg on the label and what else is in the product, and count the calcium from food before adding a supplement.

targets.label: EFSA reference intake, adults 25 and over
Amount commonly used in studies and supplements (1,200 mg)

foods.name: Sesame seeds
foods.note: Phytate and oxalate in seeds and greens reduce how much is absorbed.

foods.name: Sardines, canned, drained (eaten with the bones)

foodAmounts.verdict: Yes for most people who eat dairy or calcium-fortified foods: about 0.8 kg of semi-skimmed milk, or less than 150 g of cheddar-type cheese, covers 950 mg. Greens give far less per portion (over 1 kg of pak choi for 950 mg), and plant calcium is absorbed less well. People who eat no dairy and no fortified foods can fall short, and then every food in the table matters. Calcium from food and calcium from supplements are different interventions, and supplements add risks that food does not (see the safety information).
foodAmounts.notChecked: Food values are from the UK food composition table (McCance and Widdowson's CoFID 2021) built into this app, for the raw or boiled food named. Other foods, brands and fortified products differ.
